1. The animation shows whether an income annuity's payments keep up with US consumer prices (CPI-U). The test is stated on screen: "keeping up = buys at least the first check." A fixed first payment is the benchmark. The figure "Ruth" is an illustrative retiree. The frames are labeled "ILLUSTRATIVE," "US only," and "history, not a forecast."

2. A line marks what the first check buys, and a shaded band sits around it. Ruth's line, which I take to be what her payments buy, starts near that benchmark. It wobbles around it and then dips below it toward the right edge. The last two frames switch to a picture of Ruth beside a row of appliance-like boxes. The boxes shrink in size, and the last one is dark or greyed out. I read that as the same payment buying fewer goods over time, and the last box as a purchase she can no longer make.

3. I think it means that a fixed payment loses buying power as prices rise. The check can stay the same in dollars while buying less each year, so it fails the "keeps up" test. The animation's own caption limits this to US history and says it is not a forecast.

4. The animation gives no explicit advice, and no text tells the viewer what to choose. A viewer might infer that when comparing the two payout options, they should check whether payments adjust for inflation, and how long they might need the income to last.

5. That inference is my own conclusion. The animation never mentions the two payout options, inflation-adjusted payments, or any action to take. It only shows buying power falling relative to the first check, and it says it is not a forecast.
